notes.front: What is capital expenditure (CapEx)?
notes.back: Large, up-front investment in fixed assets, which may need lead time to procure, provision and configure.
notes.explanation: Buying and running your own data-centre hardware is the typical case the study guide contrasts with the cloud.
notes.example: Like buying a delivery van outright before the first parcel is sent.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Scaling with Google Cloud Operations”, p. 14
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is operational expenditure (OpEx)?
notes.back: Pay-as-you-go spending on the services you use: no up-front cost, but a variable bill that follows real-time usage.
notes.explanation: Spending scales up or down with how much is actually used.
notes.example: Like hiring a van by the day, only on the days you have deliveries.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Scaling with Google Cloud Operations”, p. 14
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is total cost of ownership (TCO), in a move to Google Cloud?
notes.back: The full cost of an environment, calculated during the assess phase of a migration.
notes.explanation: Calculating it sits beside taking inventory of apps, finding their dependencies and setting performance benchmarks.
notes.example: Like comparing a car's whole running cost, not just its price tag, before deciding to lease instead.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Migrate to Google Cloud: Get started”, “The migration path”
notes.evidence: Assess. In this phase, you perform a thorough assessment and discovery of your existing environment in order to understand your app and environment inventory, identify app dependencies and requirements, perform total cost of ownership calculations, and establish app performance benchmarks.

notes.front: What is cloud financial governance, as the study guide describes it?
notes.back: Managing cloud costs through a collaborative, cross-functional partnership of people, processes and technology.
notes.explanation: The exam guide's examples of good practice are identifying who manages cloud costs and using Google Cloud's cost management tools.
notes.example: Like a household budget that works only when someone owns it, reviews it monthly and tracks it in a banking app.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Scaling with Google Cloud Operations”, p. 14
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is FinOps, as Google Cloud's cost optimisation pillar refers to it?
notes.back: A cloud cost discipline whose core tenets closely match the pillar's principles; it is relevant to organisations of any size or cloud maturity.
notes.explanation: Adopting these principles is meant to help you control and optimise costs throughout your time in the cloud.
notes.example: Like a fitness plan for spending: habits and checks applied all the time rather than a one-off diet.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Well-Architected Framework: Cost optimization pillar”, “Core principles”
notes.evidence: These principles are closely aligned with the core tenets of cloud FinOps. FinOps is relevant to any organization, regardless of its size or maturity in the cloud. By adopting these principles and following the related recommendations, you can control and optimize costs throughout your journey in the cloud.

notes.front: What is the Google Cloud resource hierarchy?
notes.back: A structured way to organise cloud resources: the organisation at the top, optional folders, then projects holding the resources.
notes.explanation: Every resource except the one at the top has exactly one parent.
notes.example: Like a company filing system: the whole company, then department drawers, then project files, then the papers in them.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “About resource hierarchy”
notes.evidence: The Google Cloud resource hierarchy provides a structured way to organize your cloud resources. All resources except for the highest resource in a hierarchy have exactly one parent. The hierarchy consists of the organization (root) at the top, followed by folders (optional) for grouping, and then projects, which contain the actual service resources like Compute Engine virtual machines

notes.front: What is the organization resource (the exam guide's "organization node")?
notes.back: The resource that represents an entity, such as a company, and is the root node of the resource hierarchy.
notes.explanation: It is the parent of all folder and project resources in the hierarchy.
notes.example: Like the company's name on the front of the filing cabinet: everything inside belongs to it.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “About resource hierarchy”, “The organization resource”
notes.evidence: The organization resource represents an entity (such as a company) and serves as the root node of the Google Cloud resource hierarchy. It provides the following key functions: - The organization acts as the parent to all folder and project resources.

notes.front: What is a folder in the resource hierarchy?
notes.back: An optional grouping between the organization resource and projects; using folders requires an organization resource.
notes.explanation: Folders sit under the organization resource, with their child projects beneath them.
notes.example: Like a department drawer in the company filing cabinet.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “About resource hierarchy”, “The folder resource”
notes.evidence: Folder resources are an optional grouping mechanism between organization resources and project resources. An organization resource is required to use folders. Folder resources and their child project resources reside under the organization resource.

notes.front: What is a project in Google Cloud?
notes.back: The fundamental organising entity: you need one to use Google Cloud and its services.
notes.explanation: It is essential for using services, enabling billing, adding collaborators and managing permissions.
notes.example: Like a single project file that holds the paperwork, budget and access list for one piece of work.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “About resource hierarchy”, “The project resource”
notes.evidence: The project resource is the fundamental organizing entity. Organization and folder resources can contain multiple projects. You need a project resource to use Google Cloud. It is essential for creating, enabling, and using all Google Cloud services, managing APIs, enabling billing, adding and removing collaborators, and managing permissions.

notes.front: In the resource hierarchy, what is a resource?
notes.back: An actual service resource, such as a Compute Engine virtual machine or a storage bucket, held inside a project.
notes.explanation: Any Google Cloud resource you allocate and use must belong to a project.
notes.example: Like the individual papers inside a project file.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Google Cloud overview”, “Projects”
notes.evidence: Any Google Cloud resources that you allocate and use must belong to a project. You can think of a project as the organizing entity for what you're building.

notes.front: What are quotas in Google Cloud?
notes.back: Limits on how much of a Google Cloud resource a project can use.
notes.explanation: They help ensure fairness and reduce spikes in resource use, and also help you manage your own resources.
notes.example: Like a library limiting each member to ten books at a time.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Cloud Quotas overview”
notes.evidence: Google Cloud uses quotas to help ensure fairness and reduce spikes in resource use and availability. A quota restricts how much of a Google Cloud resource your Google Cloud project can use.

notes.front: What is a budget alert in Cloud Billing?
notes.back: An email sent when actual or forecast costs pass a percentage of a budget, set by threshold rules.
notes.explanation: Alerts keep you informed of how spending is tracking against the budget you set.
notes.example: Like a banking app texting you when you have spent 80% of the month's grocery money.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Create, edit, or delete budgets and budget alerts”
notes.evidence: You can set threshold rules to trigger email alert notifications. When your actual costs or forecasted costs exceed a percentage of your budget (based on the rules you set), alert emails are sent to the recipients you specify.

notes.front: What is a spend cap budget?
notes.back: A Cloud Billing budget type, in preview, that sets a spend cap on a project, where your service supports it.
notes.explanation: Alerts-only budgets don't cap usage or spending, so the documentation points to a spend cap budget when you need an actual limit.
notes.example: Like a prepaid card that stops working at its limit, unlike a text alert about your balance.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Create, edit, or delete budgets and budget alerts”
notes.evidence: Setting an alerts-only budget doesn't automatically cap Google Cloud or Google Maps Platform usage or spending.

notes.front: What are Cloud Billing reports?
notes.back: Reports in the Google Cloud console showing cost history, current cost trends and forecast costs.
notes.explanation: The views can be adjusted to suit different billing analysis needs.
notes.example: Like the spending charts in a banking app, broken down by shop and month.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Cloud Billing Reports”
notes.evidence: Get at-a-glance and user-configurable views of your cost history, current cost trends, and forecasted costs with intuitive reports available in the Google Cloud console. Several different reports are available for your billing data analysis needs.

notes.front: What is Dynamic Workload Scheduler (DWS)?
notes.back: A Google Cloud scheduler that creates Flex-start virtual machines on a best-effort basis when capacity is available.
notes.explanation: It schedules them according to availability and the run duration given in the request.
notes.example: Like a restaurant waiting list that seats your party as soon as a big enough table frees up.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “About resize requests in a MIG”, “How resize requests work”
notes.evidence: On a best-effort basis, the Dynamic Workload Scheduler schedules Flex-start VM creation based on availability and the run duration that is specified in the request.

notes.front: What are committed use discounts (CUDs)?
notes.back: Discounted prices for eligible resources in return for committing to a minimum usage or spend for one or three years.
notes.explanation: The commitment is a contract: a minimum level of resources or a minimum amount of spending over the term.
notes.example: Like a gym that charges less per month if you sign up for a whole year.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Committed use discounts”
notes.evidence: CUDs provide discounted prices for eligible Google Cloud resources in exchange for purchasing committed use contracts (also known as commitments). When you purchase Google Cloud commitments, you commit to either using a minimum level of resources or spending a minimum amount, for a term duration of one or three years.

notes.front: What does moving from on-premises to the cloud do to how an organisation spends, per the study guide?
notes.back: It shifts costs from capital expenditure to operational expenditure.
notes.explanation: Fixed-asset purchases give way to pay-as-you-go charges for services used.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Scaling with Google Cloud Operations”, p. 14
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does shifting from CapEx to an OpEx cloud model free teams from, per the study guide?
notes.back: The burden of buying and maintaining physical hardware, which allows agility and speed.
notes.explanation: Without hardware to procure and look after, teams can move faster.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Scaling with Google Cloud Operations”, p. 14
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Why can capital expenditure delay a project, per the study guide?
notes.back: Fixed assets may need lead time to procure, provision and configure.
notes.explanation: The money and the waiting both come before any use of the asset.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Scaling with Google Cloud Operations”, p. 14
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Is operational expenditure in the cloud a fixed or a variable cost?
notes.back: Variable: there is no up-front cost, and spending scales up or down with real-time usage.
notes.explanation: Pay-as-you-go means the bill follows use.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Scaling with Google Cloud Operations”, p. 14
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A start-up launches with no hardware purchase and pays a cloud bill that rises in its busy season. Is that CapEx or OpEx?
notes.back: OpEx: pay-as-you-go spending that varies with usage.
notes.explanation: No up-front investment and a bill that follows real usage are the marks of operational expenditure.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Scaling with Google Cloud Operations”, p. 14
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In which phase of a migration to Google Cloud are total cost of ownership calculations done?
notes.back: The assess phase.
notes.explanation: Assessment is where you study your existing environment before planning the move.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Migrate to Google Cloud: Get started”, “The migration path”
notes.evidence: Assess. In this phase, you perform a thorough assessment and discovery of your existing environment in order to understand your app and environment inventory, identify app dependencies and requirements, perform total cost of ownership calculations, and establish app performance benchmarks.

notes.front: Before deciding to migrate, a finance team wants the full cost of its current environment worked out as part of assessing it. Which calculation is that?
notes.back: A total cost of ownership (TCO) calculation.

notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Migrate to Google Cloud: Get started”, “The migration path”
notes.evidence: perform total cost of ownership calculations, and establish app performance benchmarks.

notes.front: What kind of partnership does effective cloud financial governance need, per the study guide?
notes.back: A collaborative, cross-functional one between people, processes and technology.

notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Scaling with Google Cloud Operations”, p. 14

notes.front: In cloud cost control, which of people, process and technology covers identifying who manages cloud costs?

notes.front: In cloud cost control, which of people, process and technology covers setting a routine so usage is monitored?

notes.front: In cloud cost control, which of people, process and technology covers using Google Cloud's tools for visibility, automated cost control and optimisation recommendations?
notes.back: Technology.

notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Scaling with Google Cloud Operations”, p. 14
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A company has good billing tools, but nobody is accountable for its cloud bill, so nobody acts on it. Which of people, process and technology is missing?

notes.front: Which cost optimisation principle, aligned with FinOps, says to provision only what you need and pay only for what you consume?
notes.back: Optimise resource usage.
notes.explanation: It sits beside aligning spend with business value, a culture of cost awareness, and optimising continuously.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Well-Architected Framework: Cost optimization pillar”, “Core principles”
notes.evidence: Optimize resource usage: Provision only the resources that you need, and pay only for the resources that you consume.

notes.front: From the top, the resource hierarchy runs: organization resource, folders, {{c1::projects}}, then resources.
notes.explanation: Projects hold the actual service resources, and folders group projects.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “About resource hierarchy”
notes.evidence: The Google Cloud resource hierarchy provides a structured way to organize your cloud resources. All resources except for the highest resource in a hierarchy have exactly one parent. The hierarchy consists of the organization (root) at the top, followed by folders (optional) for grouping, and then projects, which contain the actual service resources like Compute Engine virtual machines

notes.front: What is the order, from the top of the hierarchy, of: a project, a Compute Engine virtual machine, the organization resource, a folder?
notes.back: Organization resource, folder, project, virtual machine.
notes.explanation: The virtual machine is a service resource, which lives inside a project.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “About resource hierarchy”
notes.evidence: The Google Cloud resource hierarchy provides a structured way to organize your cloud resources. All resources except for the highest resource in a hierarchy have exactly one parent. The hierarchy consists of the organization (root) at the top, followed by folders (optional) for grouping, and then projects, which contain the actual service resources like Compute Engine virtual machines

notes.front: With an organization resource, what happens to a project when the employee who created it leaves?
notes.back: The organisation keeps it: projects belong to the organisation, not to the employee.
notes.explanation: Projects follow the organization resource's lifecycle.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “About resource hierarchy”, “Benefits of the organization resource”
notes.evidence: With an organization resource, your project resources belong to your organization, not to the employee who created them. This means that your organization retains project resources when an employee leaves the company.

notes.front: A company worries that staff are creating projects that central administrators cannot see or manage. What gives administrators a central view and control of all projects?
notes.back: An organization resource.
notes.choices:
A) An organization resource
B) A spend cap budget
C) Quotas
D) Cloud Billing reports
notes.choicesExplained: B: a spend cap budget limits spending on a project; it does not show all projects. C: quotas limit resource use per project. D: Cloud Billing reports analyse costs rather than giving administrative control.
notes.explanation: Organization administrators can view and manage all projects centrally, which prevents shadow projects.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “About resource hierarchy”, “Benefits of the organization resource”
notes.evidence: In addition, Organization administrators control all resources centrally. They can view and manage all project resources in your company. This prevents shadow projects or rogue administrators.

notes.front: A company wants separate areas for its finance and engineering departments, each with sub-teams, and wants each department head to administer only their own area. What should it use?
notes.back: A folder per department, with subfolders for teams.
notes.choices:
A) One project for the whole company
B) A separate organization resource per team
C) A folder per department, with subfolders for teams
D) Budget alerts per department
notes.choicesExplained: A: one project gives no separation between departments. B: an organization resource represents the whole company and is the root; teams sit below it. D: budget alerts report spending; they do not structure or delegate administration.
notes.explanation: Folders can model departments and teams, and let you delegate administration, for example full ownership of a department's resources to its head.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “About resource hierarchy”, “The folder resource”
notes.evidence: Folder resources let you delegate administration rights. For example, you can grant each department head full ownership of all Google Cloud resources in their departments.

notes.front: What are two things a project is essential for in Google Cloud?
notes.back: Any two, for example enabling billing and managing permissions.
notes.explanation: Using any Google Cloud service, and adding or removing collaborators, also need a project.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “About resource hierarchy”, “The project resource”
notes.evidence: It is essential for creating, enabling, and using all Google Cloud services, managing APIs, enabling billing, adding and removing collaborators, and managing permissions.

notes.front: A developer wants to create a Cloud Storage bucket for the first time. What must exist before the bucket can be created?
notes.back: A project.
notes.explanation: Every Google Cloud resource you allocate and use must belong to a project.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Google Cloud overview”, “Projects”
notes.evidence: Any Google Cloud resources that you allocate and use must belong to a project.

notes.front: If you set an allow policy on a folder, which resources does it apply to?
notes.back: The folder and every resource inside it.
notes.explanation: Descendant resources inherit their ancestors' allow policies; this is called policy inheritance.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “IAM overview”, “Policy inheritance”
notes.evidence: If you set an allow policy on a container resource, then the allow policy also applies to all resources in that container. This concept is called policy inheritance, because descendant resources effectively inherit their ancestor resources' allow policies.

notes.front: A networking team must manage the networks in every project across the company. What is the most efficient way to give it access?
notes.back: Grant the role once on the organization resource.
notes.choices:
A) Grant the role on each project, one at a time
B) Grant the role once on the organization resource
C) Move all networks into one new project
D) Raise the team's quotas
notes.choicesExplained: A: this works but is the manual, per-project effort that inheritance avoids. C: moving everything is unnecessary; access flows down anyway. D: quotas limit resource use; they do not grant access.
notes.explanation: A role granted at the organisation level is inherited by every folder and project beneath it.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “About resource hierarchy”, “Benefits of the organization resource”
notes.evidence: For example, you can grant the Network Admin role to your networking team at the organization level, which lets them manage all networks in all project resources in your company, instead of granting the role for each individual project resource.

notes.front: Which benefit of the resource hierarchy, per the study guide, is precise permission mapping at every level?
notes.back: Granular access control.
notes.explanation: Permissions can be set at the organisation, folder, project or resource level.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Scaling with Google Cloud Operations”, p. 14
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which benefit of the resource hierarchy, per the study guide, reduces the need to configure individual resources by hand?

notes.front: Which benefit of the resource hierarchy, per the study guide, minimises risk exposure by enforcing least privilege?
notes.back: Security and compliance.

notes.front: Which benefit of the resource hierarchy, per the study guide, simplifies compliance reviews through centralised tracking?
notes.back: Strong visibility and auditing capabilities.

notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Scaling with Google Cloud Operations”, p. 14

notes.front: Which type of quota limits how much of a resource Google Cloud allocates to you, such as the number of virtual machines in a project?
notes.back: An allocation quota.
notes.explanation: Rate quotas limit consumption over a time period, and concurrent quotas limit operations running at once.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Cloud Quotas overview”, “Types of quotas”
notes.evidence: Allocation quotas: Allocation quotas restrict how much of a resource Google Cloud allocates to you. For example, Compute Engine applies an allocation quota to the number of VMs allocated for a Google Cloud project. - Rate quotas: Rate quotas restrict the rate at which you can consume a resource.

notes.front: A team wants its test project to be technically unable to run more than a set number of virtual machines, whatever anyone tries. Which control fits?
notes.back: Quotas.
notes.choices:
A) A budget alert
B) Cloud Billing reports
C) Committed use discounts
D) Quotas
notes.choicesExplained: A: a budget alert only sends notifications; it does not stop anything. B: reports analyse costs after the fact. C: committed use discounts lower prices; they do not limit use.
notes.explanation: A quota restricts how much of a resource a project can use, and a task needing more than the quota fails.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Cloud Quotas overview”, “When you run out of quota”
notes.evidence: Usually, if you run out of quota the task that you're trying to perform fails and you get a quota error.

notes.front: What are two levels a Cloud Billing budget can apply to?
notes.back: Any two, for example a whole Cloud Billing account and one or more projects.
notes.explanation: Budgets can also cover organisations, folders, specific services, or resources with a particular label.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Create, edit, or delete budgets and budget alerts”
notes.evidence: You can define the scope of the budget. Your budget can apply at any of these levels: - An entire Cloud Billing account. - One or more organizations, folders, or projects that are associated with your Cloud Billing account.

notes.front: Does an alerts-only budget stop usage when its amount is reached?
notes.back: No. It sends alerts but doesn't automatically cap usage or spending.
notes.explanation: Alert emails may prompt you to act, but they don't prevent use or billing of services.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Create, edit, or delete budgets and budget alerts”
notes.evidence: Budget alert emails might prompt you to take action to control your costs, but they don't automatically prevent the use or billing of your services when the alerts-only budget amount or threshold rules are met or exceeded.

notes.front: A manager sets an alerts-only budget of 1,000 a month and tells finance that services will stop at that amount. Is that right?
notes.back: No. The budget only sends alerts; spending can continue past it.
notes.explanation: Alerts-only budgets don't automatically cap usage or spending; a spend cap budget, where supported, is the separate option.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Create, edit, or delete budgets and budget alerts”
notes.evidence: Setting an alerts-only budget doesn't automatically cap Google Cloud or Google Maps Platform usage or spending.

notes.front: How does a budget differ from a quota in controlling consumption?
notes.back: A budget alerts you as costs pass thresholds; a quota restricts how much of a resource a project can use.
notes.explanation: One informs; the other limits.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Create, edit, or delete budgets and budget alerts”
notes.evidence: Alerts-only budgets trigger alerts to inform you of how your usage costs are trending over time.

notes.front: What are two questions a Cloud Billing report can answer?
notes.back: Any two, for example which project cost the most last month, and which service cost the most.
notes.explanation: It can also show spending trends, forecast costs, and spend by region or label.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Cloud Billing Reports”, “Analyze your usage costs: Billing report”
notes.evidence: - Which Google Cloud project cost the most last month? - Which Google Cloud service (for example, Compute Engine or Cloud Storage) cost me the most?

notes.front: The finance director asks which Google Cloud service cost the company most last month, and what next month is likely to cost. Where should the team look?

A) Quotas

D) Cloud Billing reports

notes.explanation: The billing report can show which service cost the most and forecast future costs from historical trends.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Cloud Billing Reports”, “Analyze your usage costs: Billing report”
notes.evidence: - Which Google Cloud service (for example, Compute Engine or Cloud Storage) cost me the most? - What are my forecasted future costs based on historical trends?

notes.front: What does Dynamic Workload Scheduler do if you lack quota or resources are temporarily unavailable?
notes.back: It keeps the request until you have enough quota and the resources become available.
notes.explanation: Scheduling is best-effort, based on availability and the requested run duration.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “About resize requests in a MIG”, “How resize requests work”
notes.evidence: If you lack standard or preemptible allocation quota, or if resources are temporarily unavailable, then the Dynamic Workload Scheduler maintains the request until you have sufficient quota and resources become available.

notes.front: A research lab has a batch job that must run for five days on scarce, high-demand machines, but it can start at any time next week. Which option fits best?
notes.back: Dynamic Workload Scheduler with Flex-start virtual machines.
notes.choices:
A) A spend cap budget
B) Dynamic Workload Scheduler with Flex-start virtual machines
C) Cloud Billing reports
D) A new folder for the lab
notes.choicesExplained: A: a spend cap budget limits spending; it does not obtain machines. C: reports analyse past costs. D: a folder organises projects; it does not schedule capacity.
notes.explanation: Flex-start virtual machines suit workloads that run for up to seven days but can start at any time.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “About resize requests in a MIG”, “Use cases”
notes.evidence: These VMs are suitable for workloads that need to run for up to seven days, but can start at any time.

notes.front: For Compute Engine, how do spend-based and resource-based committed use discounts differ?
notes.back: Spend-based commitments are measured in spend per hour; resource-based ones in underlying resources such as processors and memory.
notes.explanation: You choose the type by service and by whether your resource needs are predictable.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Committed use discounts”, “Spend-based versus resource-based commitments”
notes.evidence: Spend-based commitments for Compute Engine are purchased and measured in terms of the dollars per hour of equivalent discount spend. Resource-based commitments for Compute Engine are purchased and measured in terms of the underlying vCPU, memory, GPU, and Local SSD disk resources.

notes.front: A company runs a steady workload that it expects to need at the same level for the next three years. Which option lowers what it pays?
notes.back: Committed use discounts.
notes.choices:
A) Budget alerts
B) Quotas
C) Committed use discounts
D) Cloud Billing reports
notes.choicesExplained: A: budget alerts warn about spending but do not reduce prices. B: quotas limit usage, not price. D: reports show costs; they do not change them.
notes.explanation: Committing to a minimum level of resources or spend for one or three years earns discounted prices.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Committed use discounts”
notes.evidence: When you purchase Google Cloud commitments, you commit to either using a minimum level of resources or spending a minimum amount, for a term duration of one or three years.
